cards.statement: A CloudWatch composite alarm can evaluate a rule expression built from raw metric values.
cards.explanation: A composite alarm applies a logical rule to the states of other alarms. Its inputs are alarm states such as ALARM, OK, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
cards.misconception: Composite alarms aggregate metric values rather than evaluate other alarms' states.

cards.statement: A CloudWatch alarm on a single metric can invoke a Lambda function directly as its configured alarm action.
cards.explanation: CloudWatch supports Lambda functions as alarm action targets. This provides a direct path for running custom operational actions.

cards.statement: A CloudWatch alarm on a single metric repeats its Amazon SNS action while its ALARM state persists.
cards.explanation: A CloudWatch alarm invokes its SNS action when the alarm changes state. An unchanged ALARM state does not trigger repeated SNS actions.
cards.misconception: Alarm notifications repeat whenever an alarm continues to breach its threshold.

cards.statement: A CloudWatch dashboard displays metrics from different AWS Regions together in the same operational view.
cards.explanation: CloudWatch dashboards bring metrics from different Regions into one view. Widget or metric settings identify the Region supplying the data.

cards.statement: A new CloudWatch Logs metric filter publishes metrics for matching events stored before its creation.
cards.explanation: CloudWatch Logs metric filters publish metrics for events that arrive after the filter is created. They do not backfill metrics from earlier log events.
cards.misconception: Creating a metric filter converts previously stored log events into historical metrics.

source.title: Creating metrics from log events using filters

cards.statement: A CloudWatch Logs subscription filter sends matching incoming log events to Amazon Data Firehose.
cards.explanation: Configure a subscription filter with an Amazon Data Firehose destination to forward matching incoming events from its log group.

cards.statement: CloudWatch Logs Insights discovers fields automatically in application log events that contain JSON.
cards.explanation: CloudWatch Logs Insights discovers JSON fields in application logs, so operators can query those fields rather than treating the event as plain text.

source.title: Analyzing log data with CloudWatch Logs Insights

cards.statement: An AWS CloudTrail trail records Amazon S3 object API activity by default when trail logging is enabled.
cards.explanation: S3 object API operations are CloudTrail data events. Configure data event selectors on the trail to record them.
cards.misconception: Enabling trail logging includes S3 object operations under the default event selection.

cards.statement: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus managed collectors send scraped Amazon EKS metrics over the public internet.
cards.explanation: Managed collectors scrape through network interfaces and send metrics to the workspace through a VPC endpoint. The metrics stay off the public internet.
cards.misconception: Managed Prometheus collection sends scraped metrics through a public network path.

source.title: Ingest metrics with AWS managed collectors

cards.statement: Amazon SNS starts delivering topic messages to a new email subscriber before subscription confirmation.
cards.explanation: An email recipient confirms the Amazon SNS subscription before topic messages reach that address. A pending subscription receives the confirmation request.
cards.misconception: Adding an email subscription immediately enables topic message delivery.

source.title: Amazon SNS email subscription setup and management

cards.statement: Amazon EventBridge matches literal string values in event patterns regardless of letter case by default.
cards.explanation: EventBridge compares literal strings character by character, including letter case. Case-insensitive matching uses a comparison operator.
cards.misconception: Literal string patterns ignore case.

cards.statement: Amazon EventBridge ignores extra event fields beyond those specified in a rule's event pattern.
cards.explanation: An EventBridge rule tests the fields in its event pattern. Additional fields in the incoming event do not prevent a match.

cards.statement: With a logging trail, CloudTrail sends captured API events to the default EventBridge event bus.
cards.explanation: CloudTrail events arrive on the default EventBridge event bus. A rule on that bus can forward matching events to a custom bus.

source.title: AWS service events delivered via AWS CloudTrail

cards.statement: With a logging trail, an ENABLED EventBridge rule can match read-only CloudTrail management events.
cards.explanation: Read-only CloudTrail management events need the rule state ENABLED_WITH_ALL_CLOUDTRAIL_MANAGEMENT_EVENTS. The default ENABLED state matches write management events.
cards.misconception: ENABLED rules include read-only management events.

source.title: AWS service events delivered via AWS CloudTrail

cards.statement: A Lambda function's resource-based policy can grant EventBridge permission to invoke the function.
cards.explanation: A resource-based policy that grants lambda:InvokeFunction to events.amazonaws.com authorizes the rule. EventBridge relies on it when no IAM execution role is configured on the target.

source.title: Using resource-based policies for Amazon EventBridge

cards.statement: An EventBridge rule can use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue as its target's dead-letter queue.
cards.explanation: EventBridge target dead-letter queues use Amazon SQS standard queues. FIFO queues are unsupported for this delivery-failure destination.
cards.misconception: EventBridge target dead-letter queues accept FIFO queues.

source.title: Using dead-letter queues to process undelivered events in EventBridge

cards.statement: AWS Systems Manager Automation cancels running invocations when its error threshold is reached.
cards.explanation: Automation stops starting invocations on additional targets at the error threshold. Invocations already running are allowed to finish.
cards.misconception: The error threshold cancels in-progress invocations.

cards.statement: An aws:branch step can choose its next runbook step using output from an earlier step.
cards.explanation: AWS Systems Manager Automation lets an aws:branch choice evaluate a previous step's output to select the next step.

cards.statement: AWS Health Dashboard identifies affected EC2 instances in account-specific maintenance events.
cards.explanation: Account-specific AWS Health events include affected resource information, helping an operator locate instances impacted by scheduled maintenance.

cards.statement: Operators can tune gp3 throughput independently of an Amazon EBS volume's storage capacity.
cards.explanation: gp3 separates provisioned performance from storage capacity. Operators adjust its throughput setting within the volume type's performance constraints.

source.title: Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD volumes

cards.statement: For a gp2 volume, BurstBalance measures the percentage of provisioned IOPS currently in use.
cards.explanation: BurstBalance reports the percentage of gp2 I/O credits remaining. A falling value shows that the volume is consuming its burst credits.
cards.misconception: BurstBalance measures current IOPS utilization rather than remaining burst credits.

source.title: Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD volumes

cards.statement: Amazon S3 serves standard transfers at regular bucket endpoints when S3 Transfer Acceleration is enabled.
cards.explanation: Enabling S3 Transfer Acceleration adds accelerate endpoints. The bucket's regular endpoints remain available for standard data transfer.

source.title: Configuring fast, secure file transfers using Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration

cards.statement: After a multipart upload part fails, Amazon S3 discards that upload's successfully uploaded parts.
cards.explanation: A failed multipart upload part can be retransmitted independently. Amazon S3 retains the successfully uploaded parts so the upload can continue.
cards.misconception: Failure of one part invalidates the successful parts of a multipart upload.

source.title: Uploading and copying objects using multipart upload in Amazon S3

cards.statement: By default, Amazon EFS leaves a file in the IA storage class when an application reads its content.
cards.explanation: The Transition into Standard lifecycle policy leaves accessed files in IA or Archive by default. Setting it to On first access moves them back to Standard for latency-sensitive workloads.

cards.statement: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server automatically fails over when operators change Multi-AZ throughput capacity.
cards.explanation: A Multi-AZ throughput change replaces the file servers behind the file system. Amazon FSx performs failover and failback during those replacements.
tags: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

cards.statement: Amazon S3 Files automatically loads the linked dataset into high-performance storage before serving file reads.
cards.explanation: S3 Files loads file contents on demand and keeps an active working set in high-performance storage. Mounting the file system does not copy the whole linked dataset.
cards.misconception: S3 Files imports the complete linked dataset before applications can read files.
cards.volatilityNote: S3 Files is a recently introduced service whose documented loading behavior may evolve.

cards.statement: CloudWatch Database Insights Standard mode displays per-query statistics for an Amazon RDS DB instance.
cards.explanation: CloudWatch Database Insights visualizes per-query statistics in Advanced mode. Standard mode does not provide this view.
cards.misconception: Database Insights Standard mode includes the per-query statistics visualization.
cards.volatilityNote: Database Insights mode capabilities may change as AWS expands the service.

cards.statement: An EC2 cluster placement group can place instances across Availability Zones to improve network performance.
cards.explanation: A cluster placement group packs EC2 instances close together within one Availability Zone. Its network performance benefit depends on that placement.
cards.misconception: A cluster placement group distributes instances across Availability Zones.

source.title: Placement groups for your Amazon EC2 instances

cards.statement: AWS Compute Optimizer bases EC2 recommendations on average utilization points from its sampling intervals.
cards.explanation: For EC2 instance recommendations, Compute Optimizer uses the maximum utilization point within each sampling interval rather than the interval average.
cards.misconception: Compute Optimizer smooths utilization peaks into interval averages when generating EC2 recommendations.

source.title: Metrics analyzed by AWS Compute Optimizer

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling chooses a step scaling adjustment from the size of the CloudWatch alarm breach.
cards.explanation: A step scaling policy links ranges above or below an alarm threshold to different capacity adjustments. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling selects the adjustment that matches the breach.

source.title: Step and simple scaling policies for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

cards.statement: An Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling predictive scaling policy removes instances when its forecast predicts lower demand.
cards.explanation: Predictive scaling adds capacity for forecast increases. An operator uses dynamic scaling policies to remove capacity when demand falls.
cards.misconception: Predictive scaling removes excess instances when its forecast declines.

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling keeps dynamic scaling policies active after a scheduled action changes desired capacity.
cards.explanation: Scheduled actions set group capacity at chosen times. Dynamic scaling policies continue responding to metrics afterward, within the group's capacity bounds.

source.title: Scheduled scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

cards.statement: An Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking policy can use INSUFFICIENT_DATA as a signal to reduce capacity.
cards.explanation: Target tracking pauses scaling when missing metric data puts its alarms in INSUFFICIENT_DATA. Usable metric data lets the policy resume its scaling decisions.
cards.misconception: Target tracking interprets an unknown utilization level as low demand.

source.title: Target tracking scaling policies for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

cards.statement: With cluster mode disabled, Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey balances individual queries through its reader endpoint.
cards.explanation: The Valkey reader endpoint distributes new connections among read replicas through round-robin DNS. Queries within an existing connection stay with that connection's replica.
cards.misconception: The reader endpoint balances each query instead of distributing connections.

cards.statement: Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) sends strongly consistent read requests through to DynamoDB.
cards.explanation: DAX forwards strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB and returns the response to the client. It leaves those results out of its cache.

cards.statement: Amazon CloudFront Origin Shield can merge simultaneous cache misses for an object into fewer origin requests.
cards.explanation: Origin Shield merges concurrent requests for the same uncached object. The origin receives fewer duplicate fetches during a burst of requests.

cards.statement: Amazon RDS reboots an existing read replica when the operator promotes it to a standalone DB instance.
cards.explanation: Amazon RDS restarts a read replica during promotion. The operator waits for the reboot to finish before using the standalone DB instance.

source.title: Promoting a read replica to be a standalone DB instance

cards.statement: An Aurora Serverless v2 cluster applies its maximum capacity setting to the cluster's combined compute capacity.
cards.explanation: The Aurora Serverless v2 capacity range applies separately to the writer and readers. The maximum setting bounds an individual instance's compute capacity.
cards.misconception: Aurora Serverless v2 sets a combined compute budget for the whole cluster.

cards.statement: Amazon DynamoDB auto scaling adjusts a global secondary index's provisioned capacity independently of its base table.
cards.explanation: A global secondary index has its own provisioned throughput. Its scaling policy adjusts that index's capacity separately from the base table.

source.title: Managing throughput capacity automatically with DynamoDB auto scaling

cards.statement: An Application Load Balancer takes its HTTP health check path from the target group's configuration.
cards.explanation: For HTTP targets, set HealthCheckPath to an application endpoint that answers health check requests. This setting belongs to the target group.

source.title: Health checks for Application Load Balancer target groups

cards.statement: An Application Load Balancer stops forwarding requests when all registered targets in its target group are unhealthy.
cards.explanation: An Application Load Balancer fails open when its registered targets are unhealthy across the enabled zones. It forwards requests to those targets despite their health status.
cards.misconception: An Application Load Balancer stops forwarding when its target group has no healthy registered targets.

source.title: Health checks for Application Load Balancer target groups

cards.statement: Amazon Route 53 treats a disabled child health check as healthy while it evaluates the parent calculated health check.
cards.explanation: A disabled health check that a calculated health check monitors is treated as healthy. To have Route 53 count it as unhealthy instead, an operator inverts its health check status.

source.title: Values that you specify when you create or update health checks

cards.statement: Amazon Route 53 health checkers probe an endpoint's private IP address inside an Amazon VPC.
cards.explanation: Route 53 health checkers run outside the VPC, so an endpoint checked by IP address needs a public IP. For instances with only private IPs, a health check can monitor a CloudWatch alarm instead.
cards.misconception: Route 53 endpoint health checkers reach private VPC addresses directly.

source.title: Values that you specify when you create or update health checks

cards.statement: The standby replica in an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment serves application reads during normal operation.
cards.explanation: An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance standby provides failover support. The primary instance handles application reads while the standby stays ready for recovery.
cards.misconception: An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance standby also handles normal read traffic.

source.title: Multi-AZ DB instance deployments for Amazon RDS

cards.statement: Amazon RDS automatically repoints a Multi-AZ DB instance's existing DNS record to its standby during failover.
cards.explanation: RDS changes the destination returned by the DB instance's DNS name during failover. Clients re-establish connections to resolve the updated destination.

source.title: Failing over a Multi-AZ DB instance for Amazon RDS

cards.statement: An operator can attach an Amazon EBS volume to an Amazon EC2 instance in another Availability Zone of the same Region.
cards.explanation: An EBS volume attaches to an EC2 instance in the volume's own Availability Zone. Matching the Region alone is insufficient for attachment.
cards.misconception: EBS volume attachment works across Availability Zones within a Region.

source.title: Attach an Amazon EBS volume to an Amazon EC2 instance

cards.statement: With Cross-Region Replication enabled, Amazon S3 copies matching new objects to the destination bucket asynchronously.
cards.explanation: S3 replication copies objects asynchronously after source writes. A successful write to the source bucket does not wait for the destination copy.

source.title: Replicating objects within and across Regions

cards.statement: Amazon Application Recovery Controller's zonal shift terminates existing connections to Network Load Balancer targets.
cards.explanation: Existing connections to Network Load Balancer targets persist after an ARC zonal shift. The shift stops new traffic to targets in the affected zone.
cards.misconception: Starting a zonal shift forcibly closes established Network Load Balancer target connections.

source.title: Zonal shift for your Network Load Balancer

cards.statement: On its initial failover attempt, Amazon Aurora ranks healthy replicas by instance size ahead of promotion priority.
cards.explanation: On an initial failover attempt, Aurora prefers eligible replicas by promotion priority. Instance size breaks ties within the same tier.
cards.misconception: Aurora replica size takes precedence over the configured promotion priority.

cards.statement: A root user can remove AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode after grace time ends while backups remain.
cards.explanation: Compliance mode makes the vault lock immutable after its grace period. AWS Backup rejects lock removal even when the account's root user requests it.
cards.misconception: The account's root user can override a compliance-mode vault lock after the grace period.

cards.statement: A restore testing plan makes AWS Backup automatically start restore jobs according to its configured schedule.
cards.explanation: AWS Backup follows the frequency and start time in the restore testing plan. Scheduled jobs test whether the selected recovery points restore successfully.

cards.statement: Amazon RDS point-in-time recovery rewinds the existing DB instance to the selected recovery time.
cards.explanation: Amazon RDS point-in-time recovery creates a new DB instance containing the recovered data. The source DB instance remains unchanged.
cards.misconception: Point-in-time recovery rolls the source RDS DB instance back in place.

source.title: Restoring a DB instance to a specified time for Amazon RDS

cards.statement: Amazon DynamoDB automatically carries source table tags onto a table restored through point-in-time recovery.
cards.explanation: After a DynamoDB point-in-time restore, operators reapply the table's tags. Recovery restores table data but leaves tag setup to the operator.
cards.misconception: A DynamoDB point-in-time restore carries the source table's tags onto the restored table.

cards.statement: Apart from the first, each Amazon EBS snapshot of a volume saves only blocks changed or added since the last snapshot.
cards.explanation: The first snapshot of a volume is a full snapshot. Later incremental snapshots save only new and changed blocks and reference unchanged data stored in earlier snapshots.

cards.statement: Amazon EBS invalidates a volume's later snapshots when an operator deletes an earlier snapshot of that volume.
cards.explanation: Deleting an earlier EBS snapshot preserves data referenced by later snapshots. Operators can still restore volumes from those later snapshots.
cards.misconception: Later EBS snapshots depend on keeping earlier snapshot objects available for restoration.

cards.statement: A simple DeleteObject request makes Amazon S3 add a delete marker to a versioning-enabled bucket.
cards.explanation: A simple DeleteObject request specifies no version ID. Amazon S3 makes a delete marker the current version while preserving the object's earlier versions.

cards.statement: Amazon S3 assigns null version IDs to existing object versions when an operator suspends bucket versioning.
cards.explanation: Suspending S3 Versioning preserves existing object versions and their version IDs. The changed versioning state governs future object operations.
cards.misconception: Suspending S3 Versioning changes previously assigned version IDs to null.

source.title: Working with objects in a versioning-suspended bucket

cards.statement: Backups of an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system include the shadow copies stored on it.
cards.explanation: Shadow copies are stored alongside the file system's data, so file system backups capture them. Shadow copies are off by default; an operator enables and schedules them with PowerShell commands.
tags: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

source.title: Protecting your data with shadow copies

cards.statement: In the AWS pilot light strategy, the recovery Region handles requests the moment failover begins.
cards.explanation: Pilot light keeps data stores live but application servers switched off, so the recovery Region cannot process requests until they are turned on. Warm standby serves traffic at reduced capacity immediately.
cards.misconception: A pilot light recovery Region already runs application servers that take traffic the moment it is redirected.

source.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 gives a copied AMI its own ID when an operator copies the image to another AWS Region.
cards.explanation: An AMI copied across Regions becomes a distinct image with a new identifier. The operator uses the target AMI's ID for launches in its Region.

source.title: How Amazon EC2 AMI copy works

cards.statement: EC2 Image Builder's default test workflow runs test components on the original build instance.
cards.explanation: The default test stage launches a test instance from the newly built image and runs test components there. It validates the image that the operator will distribute.
cards.misconception: The default test workflow reuses the build instance instead of launching from the completed image.

source.title: Manage build, test, and distribution workflows for Image Builder images

cards.statement: In a private repository set to IMMUTABLE, Amazon ECR stores a new image untagged when its requested tag exists.
cards.explanation: A tag collision in an IMMUTABLE repository fails with ImageTagAlreadyExistsException. Amazon ECR rejects that push instead of storing the new image as untagged.
cards.misconception: Tag immutability preserves the existing tag while accepting a colliding image as untagged.

source.title: Preventing image tags from being overwritten in Amazon ECR

cards.statement: AWS CloudFormation starts updating stack resources when an operator creates a standard change set.
cards.explanation: Creating a standard change set produces a preview of proposed changes. AWS CloudFormation changes stack resources after the operator executes the change set.
cards.misconception: Creating a change set immediately starts applying the proposed stack update.

source.title: Update CloudFormation stacks using change sets

cards.statement: A drift-aware AWS CloudFormation change set can fix drift even when the new template leaves that resource unchanged.
cards.explanation: With deployment mode REVERT_DRIFT, CloudFormation compares actual, previous and desired state. It reconciles supported drifted properties with the template's intended values.

cards.statement: AWS CloudFormation can accept a new stack update while the stack is in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED.
cards.explanation: A stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED needs recovery before another update. The operator can use ContinueUpdateRollback to restore it to UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE.
cards.misconception: A new stack update can repair UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED before rollback recovery.

cards.statement: In AWS Organizations, a service-managed StackSet with auto-deployment enabled adds stacks to new target OU accounts.
cards.explanation: With service-managed permissions and automatic deployment enabled, CloudFormation creates stacks when accounts join the targeted OU. The new accounts receive the StackSet's deployment.

source.title: Enable or disable automatic deployments for StackSets in AWS Organizations

cards.statement: AWS Service Catalog assumes a launch constraint's IAM role when an end user provisions its product.
cards.explanation: The launch role supplies permissions for provisioning the product's resources. AWS Service Catalog uses that role instead of the end user's resource permissions.

cards.statement: Amazon ECS rolling updates count RUNNING tasks for minimumHealthyPercent before essential container health checks pass.
cards.explanation: For rolling deployments, Amazon ECS waits for configured essential container health checks to pass before crediting a task toward minimumHealthyPercent. The RUNNING state alone is insufficient.
cards.misconception: RUNNING tasks satisfy the deployment's minimum healthy count before container health checks succeed.

cards.statement: Amazon ECS retains the old revision after the production traffic shift until native blue/green bake time ends.
cards.explanation: Amazon ECS keeps the previous revision running during bake time after directing production traffic to the new revision. The retained revision provides a running rollback target.

cards.statement: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager requires an inbound SSH rule to start an interactive EC2 shell session.
cards.explanation: Session Manager starts interactive shell sessions through service communication rather than inbound SSH access. Operators can keep inbound ports closed.
cards.misconception: Session Manager shell sessions depend on opening inbound SSH access to the EC2 instance.

cards.statement: With ALLOW_AS_DEPENDENCY, Patch Manager reports rejected Linux packages installed as dependencies as INSTALLED_OTHER.
cards.explanation: Patch Manager treats a rejected Linux package installed as a dependency as compliant with the baseline and records its status as INSTALLED_OTHER.

cards.statement: By default, State Manager runs a new scheduled association immediately after the operator creates it.
cards.explanation: A new State Manager association has an initial run at creation rather than waiting for the next scheduled time.

cards.statement: Parameter Store can update a String parameter by overwriting the value in its existing version.
cards.explanation: Parameter Store creates a new parameter version when its value changes. Previous versions retain their earlier values in parameter history.
cards.misconception: Parameter Store edits the current version in place rather than creating another version.

source.title: Working with parameter versions in Parameter Store

cards.statement: An AWS Systems Manager maintenance window can select managed EC2 nodes by matching resource tags.
cards.explanation: Maintenance window targets can specify tag keys and values. AWS Systems Manager selects managed nodes whose tags match those conditions.

source.title: Assign targets to a maintenance window using the console

cards.statement: Amazon S3 Event Notifications preserve the order of the object operations that generated them.
cards.explanation: Amazon S3 Event Notifications are delivered at least once and aren't guaranteed to arrive in the same order as the object operations that generated them.
cards.misconception: S3 Event Notifications preserve the sequence of the object operations that generated them.

cards.statement: For an Amazon SQS destination, S3 Event Notifications use a queue in the bucket's AWS Region.
cards.explanation: An Amazon SQS destination for S3 Event Notifications resides in the same AWS Region as the bucket that sends the notifications.

cards.statement: Amazon SQS uses visibility timeout expiration to delete a message that a consumer has received.
cards.explanation: When its visibility timeout expires, an undeleted Amazon SQS message becomes available for another processing attempt.
cards.misconception: The visibility timeout determines when SQS deletes a received message.

cards.statement: AWS Step Functions applies Catch before Retry when a state defines matching handlers for both.
cards.explanation: AWS Step Functions tries a matching Retry handler first. It checks Catch handlers if retries fail to resolve the error.
cards.misconception: A matching Catch handler takes precedence over a matching Retry handler.

source.title: Handling errors in Step Functions workflows

cards.statement: A matching explicit Deny in a role's permissions boundary overrides resource-policy access granted to its session ARN.
cards.explanation: A resource policy can grant permissions directly to an IAM role session, but an applicable explicit denial in the role's permissions boundary still blocks access.

cards.statement: An IAM permissions boundary can grant its listed Allow permissions when the operator attaches it to a role.
cards.explanation: A permissions boundary sets a ceiling for identity-based permissions. Attaching the boundary grants no permissions by itself.
cards.misconception: Attaching a permissions boundary grants the role the actions that the boundary allows.

cards.statement: A role trust policy can delegate role assumption to another AWS account by allowing that account's root ARN.
cards.explanation: An account root ARN names the trusted account, rather than just its root user. The account's administrators grant role-assumption permission to its IAM identities.

cards.statement: An IAM password expiration policy revokes a user's active access keys when the password expires.
cards.explanation: IAM password expiration affects console sign-in. An IAM user can continue making programmatic requests with active access keys after the password expires.
cards.misconception: Expiration of an IAM console password also invalidates the user's access keys.

source.title: Set an account password policy for IAM users

cards.statement: With its zone of trust set to the account, IAM Access Analyzer trusts other accounts in the same organization.
cards.explanation: An external access analyzer scoped to an account trusts that account's principals. Principals in another organization member account remain outside its zone of trust.
cards.misconception: An account-scoped external access analyzer automatically extends trust to the account's organization.

cards.statement: The IAM policy simulator automatically uses the requester's IP address to evaluate aws:SourceIp conditions.
cards.explanation: Operators supply aws:SourceIp as simulation input. The IAM policy simulator evaluates that supplied value rather than obtaining an IP address from a production request.
cards.misconception: The IAM policy simulator automatically fills aws:SourceIp from the caller's live request context.

source.title: IAM policy testing with the IAM policy simulator

cards.statement: A CloudTrail event history search returns management events from the AWS Region that the operator selects.
cards.explanation: CloudTrail event history searches cover an account within a selected Region. Operators inspect another Region separately when auditing activity there.

cards.statement: In AWS Organizations, SCPs attached to the organization root restrict IAM roles in the management account.
cards.explanation: SCPs leave users and roles in the AWS Organizations management account unaffected. Attaching an SCP to the organization root does not remove this exemption.
cards.misconception: An SCP attached to the organization root also restricts IAM roles in the management account.

cards.statement: In AWS Organizations, IAM Identity Center automatically creates IAM roles for assigned permission sets.
cards.explanation: Assigning account access through a permission set makes IAM Identity Center provision corresponding roles in the assigned accounts, with the permission set's policies.

source.title: Manage AWS accounts with permission sets

cards.statement: AWS Trusted Advisor's Security Groups – Specific Ports Unrestricted check evaluates only IPv4 inbound rules.
cards.explanation: This Trusted Advisor check evaluates IPv4 ingress rules. Operators review IPv6 ingress separately rather than treating its result as an IPv6 exposure assessment.
cards.volatilityNote: Trusted Advisor check coverage may expand; the current check evaluates IPv4 inbound rules.

source.title: Security checks: Security Groups – Specific Ports Unrestricted

cards.statement: In AWS Organizations, AWS Config scopes conformance pack deployment to the Region of the deployment request.
cards.explanation: Organization conformance pack deployment is regional. Operators issue separate deployment requests in additional Regions to establish the pack there.

source.title: Managing Conformance Packs for AWS Config Across all Accounts in Your Organization

cards.statement: In AWS Organizations, an enabled AWS Control Tower detective control evaluates unenrolled accounts in its OU.
cards.explanation: Control Tower detective controls apply to enrolled accounts in a registered OU. Accounts in that OU that remain unenrolled fall outside those controls.
cards.misconception: OU membership alone brings an account under an enabled Control Tower detective control.

cards.statement: Amazon Macie creates a new finding when a later discovery run detects sensitive data in the same S3 object.
cards.explanation: Repeated discovery of sensitive data in the same S3 object produces a separate sensitive data finding. Macie treats subsequent discoveries as new findings.

cards.statement: An IAM policy can grant access to an AWS KMS key independently of that key's key policy.
cards.explanation: An IAM policy's Allow has an effect on KMS key access when the key policy enables IAM policies. The default key policy includes that delegation.
cards.misconception: An IAM Allow grants KMS key access regardless of whether the key policy enables IAM policies.

cards.statement: AWS KMS can automatically select older key material to decrypt ciphertext created before that key's rotation.
cards.explanation: AWS KMS uses the key material that originally encrypted the ciphertext. Rotating the key material preserves decryption of earlier ciphertext.

cards.statement: ACM rechecks public DNS validation CNAME records when renewing an in-use DNS-validated certificate.
cards.explanation: ACM checks that the certificate is in use and that its validation CNAME records resolve publicly. Keeping those records in place supports managed renewal.

source.title: Renewal for domains validated by DNS

cards.statement: ACM automatically renews an imported certificate when an operator associates it with an Application Load Balancer.
cards.explanation: ACM provides no managed renewal for imported certificates. Operators obtain a renewed certificate from its issuer and import the replacement.
cards.misconception: Associating an imported certificate with an AWS service makes it eligible for ACM managed renewal.

source.title: Import certificates into AWS Certificate Manager

cards.statement: With alternating users rotation, an operator who changes the original user's permissions must also update the clone.
cards.explanation: Secrets Manager creates the clone with the original user's permissions during the first rotation. Later permission changes to the original user do not carry over to the clone.

cards.statement: AWS Secrets Manager can rotate a replica secret independently while its replication link remains active.
cards.explanation: A replica secret can't be updated independently of its primary, apart from its KMS key. To turn on rotation for a replica, an operator promotes it to a standalone secret.
cards.misconception: An active replica secret has a rotation schedule independent of its primary secret.

source.title: Promote a replica secret to a standalone secret in AWS Secrets Manager

cards.statement: Parameter Store read access to a SecureString parameter also grants decryption access to its customer managed KMS key.
cards.explanation: Reading a decrypted SecureString value requires kms:Decrypt permission on its encryption key in addition to Parameter Store read access.
cards.misconception: Permission to retrieve a SecureString parameter supplies the separate KMS decryption authorization.

source.title: Restricting decryption of SecureString parameter values

cards.statement: AWS Security Hub CSPM requires AWS Config recording to generate most security control findings.
cards.explanation: Most Security Hub CSPM controls use AWS Config service-linked rules. Enable AWS Config and record the relevant resources for those controls to produce findings.

source.title: Introduction to AWS Security Hub CSPM

cards.statement: AWS Security Hub can express exposure findings in the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF).
cards.explanation: AWS Security Hub generates exposure findings using OCSF. Operators use that schema when consuming or analyzing these findings.

cards.statement: A suppression rule makes Amazon GuardDuty automatically stop generating findings that match its criteria.
cards.explanation: GuardDuty continues generating findings that match a suppression rule. The rule automatically archives those findings rather than stopping their detection.
cards.misconception: A suppression rule turns off detection for the finding criteria it matches.

cards.statement: For identical destination CIDRs, a VPC route table prefers a static route over a propagated VPN route.
cards.explanation: When destination CIDRs match, a static VPC route takes priority over a route propagated from a virtual private gateway.

cards.statement: An EC2 security group can admit replies to an allowed inbound TCP connection despite restrictive outbound rules.
cards.explanation: Security groups track permitted connections. Reply traffic for an allowed inbound connection passes the security group regardless of its outbound rules.

source.title: Control traffic to your AWS resources using security groups

cards.statement: A VPC network ACL applies a matching deny rule even when a lower-numbered rule allows the same inbound traffic.
cards.explanation: A network ACL evaluates rules from the lowest rule number and applies the first match. A later deny rule does not override an earlier matching allow rule.
cards.misconception: Network ACL deny rules take precedence over matching allow rules regardless of rule order.

source.title: Control subnet traffic with network access control lists

cards.statement: An S3 gateway endpoint route takes matching traffic ahead of a default route to a zonal NAT gateway.
cards.explanation: Requests selected by the S3 gateway endpoint route use the endpoint rather than the default zonal NAT route. Those requests avoid NAT processing.

cards.statement: An interface VPC endpoint policy replaces its security group's inbound rules for service connectivity.
cards.explanation: An endpoint policy controls access to service operations and resources. The endpoint network interface's security group separately controls incoming network traffic.
cards.misconception: Authorizing service access through an endpoint policy also supplies inbound network access.

source.title: Access an AWS service using an interface VPC endpoint

cards.statement: An active VPC peering connection supports routing onward through its peer's other peering connections.
cards.explanation: VPC peering carries traffic between directly paired VPCs. A peer VPC does not provide transit onward through another peering connection.
cards.misconception: Routes through an intermediate VPC make peering connections transitive.

cards.statement: A virtual private gateway distributes AWS Site-to-Site VPN egress traffic across equal-cost tunnel paths.
cards.explanation: A virtual private gateway selects a primary VPN tunnel for egress traffic. Equal-cost multipath routing is unavailable for Site-to-Site VPN connections on that gateway.
cards.misconception: Equal-cost VPN tunnels let a virtual private gateway distribute egress traffic across them.

source.title: Route tables and AWS Site-to-Site VPN route priority

cards.statement: Amazon VPC IPAM reports an overlap conflict for VPC CIDRs in different private scopes when their ranges intersect.
cards.explanation: Separate IPAM private scopes represent isolated address spaces. Operators can reuse private CIDRs across unconnected networks in different scopes.
cards.misconception: IPAM detects private address conflicts across its separate private scopes.

cards.statement: With a DNS Firewall rule group associated, Route 53 Resolver passes queries through during firewall failure by default.
cards.explanation: With a DNS Firewall rule group associated, the default failure mode is closed. Route 53 Resolver returns SERVFAIL when DNS Firewall fails to reply.
cards.misconception: DNS Firewall defaults to allowing queries through during an evaluation failure.

cards.statement: In a web ACL, AWS WAF can still block a request after an earlier matching rule takes the Count action.
cards.explanation: Count records a rule match and continues evaluation. A later rule or the web ACL's default action can block a request already counted by an earlier rule.

source.title: Using rule actions in AWS WAF

cards.statement: Operators can route subnet traffic through AWS Network Firewall by targeting its endpoint in VPC route tables.
cards.explanation: After creating a firewall, operators update VPC route tables to send the traffic they want inspected through its firewall endpoints.

source.title: VPC route table configuration for AWS Network Firewall

cards.statement: Creating a Route 53 private hosted zone automatically associates the account's other VPCs in that Region.
cards.explanation: VPC associations control which VPCs resolve the zone's records through their local Resolver. Creating the zone leaves the account's other VPCs available for explicit association.
cards.misconception: Creating a private hosted zone grants private DNS resolution to other VPCs in the same account and Region.

cards.statement: A Route 53 alias A record can point the hosted zone's apex to an Application Load Balancer.
cards.explanation: Route 53 permits an alias A record at the zone apex to target an Application Load Balancer, letting the root domain resolve to the load balancer.

source.title: Choosing between alias and non-alias records

cards.statement: For unmapped client IP addresses, Amazon Route 53 selects the nearest configured geolocation record.
cards.explanation: A default geolocation record handles queries from IP addresses that Route 53 cannot map to a location. Without that default, Route 53 returns no answer for those queries.
cards.misconception: Unmapped client IPs fall back to the geographically nearest configured geolocation record.

cards.statement: Route 53 assumes a multivalue answer record is healthy when the operator leaves its health check unassigned.
cards.explanation: A multivalue answer record with no associated health check counts as healthy. Route 53 uses that assumed health when choosing records for DNS answers.

cards.statement: With public DNS query logging enabled, Route 53 can send query logs directly to an Amazon S3 bucket.
cards.explanation: Route 53 delivers public DNS query logs to CloudWatch Logs. Operators can export those logs from CloudWatch Logs to Amazon S3.
cards.misconception: Route 53 public query logging delivers directly to an S3 bucket.

cards.statement: When associated rules for a domain and its subdomain both match, Route 53 Resolver uses the subdomain rule.
cards.explanation: Resolver chooses the rule with the more specific matching domain. A matching subdomain rule takes precedence over its parent-domain rule.

source.title: How VPC Resolver determines whether the domain name in a query matches any rules

cards.statement: For SSE-KMS objects in an S3 origin, CloudFront OAC requires a KMS key policy granting the distribution access.
cards.explanation: The KMS key policy grants the CloudFront service principal permission to use the key for the specified distribution's SSE-KMS objects.

source.title: Restrict access to an Amazon S3 origin

cards.statement: For an origin in Europe (Ireland), CloudFront uses a viewer certificate from ACM in Europe (Ireland).
cards.explanation: CloudFront uses ACM certificates from US East (N. Virginia) for viewer HTTPS, regardless of the origin's Region.
cards.misconception: A CloudFront viewer certificate in ACM belongs in the same Region as the origin.

source.title: Requirements for using SSL/TLS certificates with CloudFront

cards.statement: A CloudFront origin request policy can add selected viewer cookies to the cache key independently of a cache policy.
cards.explanation: An origin request policy forwards selected cookies to the origin. The cache policy separately determines which cookies form part of the cache key.
cards.misconception: Cookies selected in an origin request policy also become part of CloudFront's cache key.

source.title: Control origin requests with a policy

cards.statement: AWS Global Accelerator releases an accelerator's assigned static IP addresses when an operator disables the accelerator.
cards.explanation: Assigned IP addresses remain with an accelerator while it exists, including while disabled. Deleting the accelerator releases its assigned addresses.
cards.misconception: Disabling an accelerator releases its assigned addresses as deleting it does.

cards.statement: VPC Reachability Analyzer sends test packets through the selected path to identify its blocking component.
cards.explanation: VPC Reachability Analyzer models network configuration instead of sending packets. A blocked result identifies a component in that configuration.
cards.misconception: Reachability Analyzer discovers blocked paths by sending test traffic through the network.

cards.statement: VPC Flow Logs can record REJECT for packets that reach a network interface after their connection has closed.
cards.explanation: A REJECT entry in VPC Flow Logs can result from packets arriving after the connection closes. The entry alone does not prove that a filtering rule is wrong.

cards.statement: For legacy access logs, an Application Load Balancer can write to an Amazon S3 bucket in a different Region.
cards.explanation: Legacy access logs use an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region as the Application Load Balancer.
cards.misconception: Legacy Application Load Balancer log delivery accepts an S3 bucket regardless of its Region.

source.title: Enable access logs for your Application Load Balancer

cards.statement: AWS WAF can redact sampled request fields through the RedactedFields setting in its logging configuration.
cards.explanation: AWS WAF's RedactedFields setting changes traffic logs and leaves sampled requests unaffected. Use web ACL data protection to mask sampled request data.
cards.misconception: Field redaction configured for AWS WAF logs also redacts request samples.

cards.statement: With delivery permissions configured, CloudFront standard logging (v2) can send logs to a CloudWatch Logs log group.
cards.explanation: CloudFront standard logging (v2) uses CloudWatch vended logs for delivery. Set a CloudWatch Logs log group's ARN as the destination.

cards.statement: CloudFront real-time logging can use an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream as its configured endpoint.
cards.explanation: CloudFront real-time log configurations name a stream in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams as their endpoint. Amazon Data Firehose can consume that stream for onward delivery.
cards.misconception: A Firehose delivery stream is a direct endpoint for CloudFront real-time access logs.

cards.statement: With a positive minimum TTL, CloudFront skips caching otherwise cacheable successful Cache-Control: private responses.
cards.explanation: CloudFront caches otherwise cacheable successful responses for its minimum TTL even when the origin marks them private. A positive minimum TTL overrides that directive.
cards.misconception: The origin's private cache directive overrides CloudFront's positive minimum TTL.
cards.volatilityNote: This behavior depends on minimum TTL being greater than zero, a numeric configuration condition.

cards.statement: For a virtual private gateway, AWS Site-to-Site VPN keeps propagated routes while an interrupted connection stays UP.
cards.explanation: An AWS Site-to-Site VPN interruption can leave propagated routes in place while the connection stays UP. Operators may need to disable route propagation to remove those routes.

source.title: Get started with AWS Site-to-Site VPN

cards.statement: Network Flow Monitor collects TCP performance metrics from agents that operators install on Amazon EC2 instances.
cards.explanation: The Network Flow Monitor agent gathers TCP connection statistics on the instance and sends them to the service for analysis.

cards.statement: Internet Monitor bases its performance comparisons for application clients on AWS's network-wide connectivity data.
cards.explanation: Internet Monitor builds its reference from measurements across AWS's global network, then applies it to traffic for the monitor's configured resources.

cards.statement: Network Synthetic Monitor sends its probes from on-premises hosts toward destinations inside Amazon VPC subnets.
cards.explanation: For Network Synthetic Monitor, choose a VPC subnet as the probe's AWS source and an on-premises IP address as its destination.
cards.misconception: Network Synthetic Monitor originates its probe traffic on-premises and sends it toward AWS.
